learning_goal: Trace each ureter from the pelviureteric junction to the bladder in its three parts, name the three constrictions and the vertebral levels at which they sit, say what crosses the ureter in the abdomen and in the pelvis in the male and the female, describe its segmental blood supply and why it is stripped at surgery, and use all of that to explain loin-to-groin colic and the operations in which a ureter is injured.

terms: bifurcation of the common iliac artery
oblique passage through the bladder wall

structures.name: right ureter
structures.label: Right ureter
structures.narration: About twenty-five centimetres long, a muscular tube of roughly three millimetres bore that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. It is retroperitoneal for its whole length and is divided for teaching into three parts of about equal share: an abdominal part on psoas major, a pelvic part on the lateral pelvic wall, and a short intramural part running obliquely through the bladder wall. The right ureter begins behind the second part of the duodenum, so a stone in its upper end can be mistaken for duodenal pain. Lower down it lies behind the right colic and ileocolic vessels and behind the terminal ileum and the root of the mesentery — which is why an inflamed retrocaecal appendix sitting on it produces pus cells and red cells in the urine and mimics a stone.

structures.name: left ureter
structures.label: Left ureter
structures.narration: The mirror image on the left, and the one more often injured in general surgery. It is crossed by the left colic vessels and then runs behind the sigmoid colon and its mesentery, entering the pelvis at the apex of the sigmoid mesocolon in the intersigmoid recess — a fold the surgeon uses deliberately to find it. Anterior resection of the rectum and sigmoid colectomy are the operations in which the left ureter is at risk, and that is why it is identified and followed before the mesentery is divided.

structures.name: right kidney
structures.label: Right kidney — where it begins
structures.narration: The ureter is the kidney's outflow. The renal pelvis funnels down inside the hilum and narrows at the pelviureteric junction — the first constriction — at about the level of L2 on the right. Obstruction here dilates the pelvis and calyces and produces a hydronephrosis with no dilated ureter below it, which is how a plain scan tells the level of a blockage without any dye.

structures.name: left kidney
structures.label: Left kidney
structures.narration: The left kidney sits half a vertebral body higher than the right, so its pelviureteric junction lies a little above the right one, at about the lower border of L1. The difference is small but it is the reason the two ureters are never quite level on a film.

structures.name: urinary bladder
structures.label: Urinary bladder — the third constriction
structures.narration: The ureter does not enter the bladder head-on. It pierces the muscular wall obliquely and runs about two centimetres within it before opening at the ureteric orifice, at the upper lateral corner of the trigone. That oblique intramural course is a flap valve: as the bladder fills, the rising pressure squeezes the tunnel shut and urine cannot go back up. A short or straight tunnel — the common congenital fault — lets urine reflux to the kidney with every void, and repeated reflux of infected urine is what scars a child's kidney. The intramural part is also the narrowest point of the whole tube, so it is where a stone that has travelled the entire ureter finally arrests, giving suprapubic pain, strangury and frequency instead of loin pain.

structures.name: right deferent duct
structures.label: Vas deferens (right)
structures.narration: The male counterpart of the uterine artery's crossing. The vas passes above the ureter on its way to the base of the bladder — water under the bridge on this side too, and the reason the ureter is at risk in pelvic surgery in both sexes.

structures.name: right psoas major
structures.label: Psoas major (right) — the abdominal bed
structures.narration: The abdominal part of the ureter runs vertically downwards on the front of psoas major, in the extraperitoneal fat, crossing the tips of the lumbar transverse processes. Because it lies on the muscle and not on the vertebral bodies, a ureter is displaced laterally by a psoas abscess and medially by a retroperitoneal fibrosis pulling it in. Between muscle and ureter runs the genitofemoral nerve, which is one reason ureteric pain radiates into the groin and scrotum.

structures.name: left psoas major
structures.label: Psoas major (left)
structures.narration: The same bed on the left. On a plain KUB film the psoas outline is the landmark against which the radiologist looks for a ureteric stone, because the abdominal ureter runs just lateral to the lumbar transverse processes and overlies that shadow.

structures.name: fifth lumbar vertebra
structures.label: Fifth lumbar vertebra — the level of the brim
terms: bifurcation of the common iliac artery
structures.narration: The lumbar transverse processes are the line to follow on a film: the ureter runs across their tips from L2 down to L5. At the level of the sacroiliac joint the ureter reaches the pelvic brim, and that is the landmark for the second constriction.

structures.name: sacrum
structures.label: Sacrum — the sacroiliac joint on the film
structures.narration: The ureteric line on a plain film runs down the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, over the sacroiliac joint, out along the lateral wall of the pelvis to the ischial spine, and then turns medially to the bladder. Any calcified density on that line is a ureteric stone until proven otherwise; anything off it, particularly the small round ones low in the pelvis, is usually a phlebolith.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: The side wall of the pelvis, which the ureter runs down. One feature on it matters here: the ischial spine.

structures.label: Ischial spine
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT — coccygeus arises from the ischial spine (gaps 0.34mm · 1 witness)
structures.narration: In the pelvis the ureter runs downwards and backwards on the lateral wall, in front of the internal iliac artery, as far as the ischial spine. There it turns sharply forwards and medially to reach the bladder. That right-angled turn at the spine is the single most useful landmark for finding the pelvic ureter at operation, and it is where the ureter is closest to the structures that endanger it.

structures.name: right common iliac artery
structures.label: Common iliac artery (right) — the second constriction
terms: crosses in front of the bifurcation
structures.narration: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim in front of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, at the level of the sacroiliac joint. Kinking over that firm vessel is the second of the three constrictions, and it is the commonest place for a stone of moderate size to hang up. The relation runs the other way at operation: find the bifurcation and the ureter is the cord crossing it, and it is the cord that shows a slow worm-like contraction when you pinch it — an artery pulsates, a ureter peristalses.

structures.name: left common iliac artery
structures.label: Common iliac artery (left)
structures.narration: The same crossing on the left. Both ureters enter the pelvis over the bifurcation, so a bilateral hydronephrosis with both ureters dilated to the brim and no further points to disease at that level — most often retroperitoneal fibrosis or nodal disease dragging them medially.

structures.name: right internal iliac artery
structures.label: Internal iliac artery (right) — the pelvic supply
structures.narration: In the pelvis the ureter runs in front of the internal iliac artery and takes its blood from that artery's branches — vesical, uterine, middle rectal. Note the direction: in the abdomen the ureter is fed from the medial side, in the pelvis from the lateral side. That reversal is the practical rule for mobilising it — dissect a ureter on the side its vessels are not coming from.

structures.name: left internal iliac artery
structures.label: Internal iliac artery (left)
structures.narration: On the left the same artery gives the uterine artery in the female, and it is that branch which crosses above the ureter about two centimetres lateral to the cervix — water under the bridge. Clamping the uterine pedicle blind at hysterectomy is how the ureter is most often tied.

structures.name: right renal artery
structures.label: Renal artery (right) — the upper supply
structures.narration: The upper third of the ureter is supplied by branches of the renal artery. The whole tube gets its blood segmentally — renal above, gonadal and aortic in the middle, vesical and uterine below — and those segments join in a fine longitudinal plexus running in the adventitia. That plexus is the reason a ureter survives being mobilised along its length but dies if it is stripped bare of its adventitia, which is the commonest cause of a leak or a stricture after pelvic surgery.

structures.name: left renal artery
structures.label: Renal artery (left)
structures.narration: The same on the left. Handle the ureter by the fat around it, never with a grasper on the wall.

structures.name: descending aorta
structures.label: Aorta — the medial neighbour
structures.narration: The abdominal aorta lies medial to the left ureter and divides at L4, just above the brim. Two aortic problems present as ureteric ones: an inflammatory aneurysm and retroperitoneal fibrosis both wrap the ureters and pull them medially, so a urogram showing ureters dragged towards the midline with obstruction is a retroperitoneal diagnosis, not a stone.

structures.name: inferior vena cava
structures.label: Inferior vena cava — medial to the right ureter
structures.narration: The cava lies immediately medial to the right ureter along its abdominal course. A developmental variant in which the right ureter passes behind the cava and hooks around it — the retrocaval or circumcaval ureter — produces a fish-hook deformity on urography and obstruction of the upper third in a young adult with no stone.

structures.name: prostate
structures.label: Prostate — the male pelvic relation
structures.narration: Sits under the bladder base, just below where the ureters enter. In the male the vas deferens is the structure that crosses above the ureter near the bladder — the male counterpart of the uterine artery. Clinically the prostate matters here because chronic outflow obstruction raises bladder pressure, defeats the flap valve at the vesicoureteric junction and backs up both ureters: bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis in an older man is a bladder outlet problem until you have excluded it.

structures.name: right seminal vesicle
structures.label: Seminal vesicle — behind the bladder base
structures.narration: Lies on the back of the bladder base lateral to the ampulla of the vas, immediately medial to where the ureter pierces the wall. It is the marker used at radical prostatectomy for how close the dissection has come to the ureteric orifice.

views.title: One tube, three parts
views.narration: The ureter is a twenty-five centimetre muscular tube, retroperitoneal from end to end, carrying urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. Divide it into three parts and everything else follows. The abdominal part runs down on psoas major from the pelviureteric junction to the pelvic brim. The pelvic part runs on the lateral pelvic wall from the brim to the bladder. The intramural part is the last two centimetres, inside the bladder wall itself. Its wall has three coats — an inner transitional epithelium that tolerates urine, a middle smooth muscle coat that generates peristalsis, and an outer adventitia carrying the blood supply. Note what it is not: it is not a passive drainpipe. Urine is pushed along it in waves at one to five a minute, and a tube that has to push against an obstruction is a tube that produces colic.

views.title: The course, and what crosses it

ops.kind: the ureter crosses in front of the bifurcation
the vas crosses above the ureter — water under the bridge in the male

views.narration: Follow it down. From the pelviureteric junction the ureter runs vertically on psoas major, across the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, with the gonadal vessels crossing in front of it obliquely — a stone patient's pain and a varicocele are neighbours for a reason. On the right it starts behind the second part of the duodenum and is crossed by the right colic and ileocolic vessels and the root of the mesentery; on the left it is crossed by the left colic vessels and disappears behind the sigmoid mesocolon. At the pelvic brim it crosses in front of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, at the level of the sacroiliac joint. In the pelvis it runs backwards and downwards on the lateral wall in front of the internal iliac artery, as far as the ischial spine, then turns forwards and medially to the bladder. The last crossing is the examinable one and it differs by sex. In the female the uterine artery crosses above it about two centimetres lateral to the cervix — water under the bridge — and the ureter there lies close to the lateral fornix of the vagina. In the male the vas deferens crosses above it in the same place. On a plain film the whole course is a line: transverse process tips, sacroiliac joint, ischial spine, then medially to the bladder.

views.title: Three constrictions and a wave
views.narration: Three places narrow, and a stone stops at one of them. First, the pelviureteric junction, where the funnel of the renal pelvis becomes a three-millimetre tube. Second, the pelvic brim, where the ureter kinks forwards over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. Third, the intramural part passing obliquely through the bladder wall — the narrowest of all. Learn them as start, brim, entry. Now the mechanism. Smooth muscle in the wall contracts in waves that begin at pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis and travel down at two to three centimetres a second, squeezing a bolus of urine ahead of them. When a stone blocks the lumen the wave meets an obstruction, the ureter above distends, and the pain that follows rises to a peak over minutes and then eases — colic, not constant pain. The patient with ureteric colic cannot lie still; the patient with peritonitis will not move. That single observation separates them at the bedside. The distension is also why an obstructed ureter dilates first, then the pelvis and calyces above it: hydroureter, then hydronephrosis, and after a few weeks of unrelieved obstruction the kidney is permanently damaged.

views.title: Segmental blood, and why the surgeon leaves the fat on

ops.kind: middle third supplied from the medial side
pelvic third supplied from the lateral side

views.narration: The ureter has no artery of its own. It is fed segmentally along its length: the upper third from the renal artery, the middle third from the gonadal artery and small branches straight off the aorta and the common iliac, the lower third from the vesical and uterine arteries of the internal iliac. Those segments anastomose in a delicate longitudinal plexus that runs in the adventitia — the sheath of fat and areolar tissue on the outside of the tube. Two rules come out of that and both are surgical. First, direction: in the abdomen the blood comes from medially, in the pelvis from laterally, so mobilise a ureter from the side its vessels are not on. Second, never strip it. A ureter can be lifted along a long stretch and will survive on its longitudinal plexus, but a ureter cleaned bare of adventitia loses that plexus and goes on to leak or to stricture weeks later. Venous and lymphatic drainage follow the arteries, and the lymph goes to the lateral aortic and iliac nodes — which is why ureteric and upper tract tumours are staged by those node groups. The nerve supply is autonomic from the renal, aortic and hypogastric plexuses, with afferents entering the cord from T11 to L2, and that segmental range is exactly the dermatome band of the pain.

views.title: Colic, and the ureters people cut

ops.kind: uterine artery crosses above — water under the bridge
outflow obstruction backs up both ureters

views.narration: Read the clinic off the course. Renal colic: severe loin pain radiating to the groin, the scrotum or the labium, colicky, with a restless patient and microscopic haematuria. The site of the pain tracks the stone — loin for the upper ureter, iliac fossa as it crosses the brim, groin and genitalia lower down, and suprapubic pain with frequency and strangury once it reaches the intramural part. That is referred pain along T11 to L2 — one segment lower than the kidney's own T10 to L1, and that difference is the loin-to-groin march itself: pain that starts at the kidney's levels in the loin drops with the stone into the ureter's lower ones. It is why renal colic can be mistaken for appendicitis on the right and diverticulitis on the left. Most stones under five millimetres pass; larger ones and any obstructed infected kidney need drainage — a stent or a nephrostomy — as an emergency, because an obstructed infected system is the one that kills. Now injury. Four operations account for most ureteric damage: hysterectomy, where the ureter is clamped with the uterine pedicle two centimetres lateral to the cervix; anterior resection and sigmoid colectomy, where the left ureter lies behind the mesocolon; ovarian surgery at the pelvic brim, where the ureter is under the suspensory ligament with the ovarian vessels; and any pelvic operation for a large mass that has dragged the ureter out of place. A ureter tied is recognised late — loin pain and a rising creatinine or urine leaking from the wound. Which is why the rule in pelvic surgery is not to avoid the ureter but to see it, follow it, and know that the peristalsing cord crossing the iliac bifurcation is the one you must not cut.

gaps: The three constrictions have no models and no anchors. They are the single most examinable fact about the ureter and the student can only hear them, not click them. FMA15571 and FMA15572 ARE now in the local decimated set — the earlier note here saying they were not is corrected as of the 2026-08-29 audit — so two of the three are measurable and one is not. The pelviureteric junction is a contact point (ureter against renal pelvis, and the renal pelvis has no separate mesh, so the nearest witness is the ureter's own proximal extreme) and the vesicoureteric junction is a contact point (ureter against bladder, FMA15900, which is in hand). The pelvic-brim constriction is neither a contact nor a positional extreme — the ureter merely kinks over the iliac bifurcation without touching it in the mesh — so it fits neither definition derive-landmark.mjs supports and must not be placed by eye. Deriving the two junctions is the honest next step; the brim constriction stays narrated.

The gonadal vessels are not in the catalog — re-searched at the 2026-08-29 audit under 'gonad', 'testicular' and 'ovarian', all three returning nothing. The testicular and ovarian vessels crossing the ureter obliquely are a named relation in every syllabus and cannot be drawn, so beat two asserts the crossing in narration only.

There is no uterus, no cervix, no vagina, no broad ligament, no ovary and no uterine artery in the catalog — re-searched at the 2026-08-29 audit under 'uter', 'cervi', 'vagin', 'ovary', 'ovarian' and 'broad ligament'; the only hits for 'cervi' are cervical vertebrae and neck muscles. The water-under-the-bridge relation — the commonest cause of surgical ureteric injury — is therefore taught through the internal iliac artery and words alone, which is the weakest part of this scene. A female pelvis model, or a companion diagram-mode scene of the uterine artery crossing, is the highest-value addition for this structure.

RESOLVED. The male counterpart of that crossing used to be narrated against the seminal vesicle and prostate because the vas was thought absent. It is in the catalog under the anatomical name 'right deferent duct' (FMA19235), it is in meshes-lite, and it is now authored as `vas_r` and shown in beat two with an explicit relationship to the right ureter. Only the left vas is still absent from the scene; the crossing is symmetrical and one side carries the teaching.

The renal pelvis has no separate model, so the pelviureteric junction is shown only as the point where the ureter mesh begins. Hydronephrosis and hydroureter cannot be shown as dilatation, only described.

The ureteric orifices, the interureteric bar and the trigone are not modelled — the bladder is one solid mesh. The oblique intramural course and the flap-valve mechanism, and therefore vesicoureteric reflux, are narrated over the outside of the bladder. A cut-open bladder base is what this beat actually needs.
The vesical and middle rectal arteries are absent, so the lower segmental supply is taught through the internal iliac trunk as a whole.

This scene does not claim to cover 'Kidney', 'Abdominal aorta & IVC' or 'Urinary bladder', although all appear in it as relations. The bladder is here as the ureter's destination and its flap valve, not as a structure with a trigone, a sphincter mechanism and micturition, and it remains on the worklist under Pelvis & Perineum.

The hip bone shown is the right one, used to teach the ischial spine turn on both sides. The teaching point is the level and the direction of the turn rather than the side, and the narration says so, but a student rotating the scene will see only one lateral wall.
